findings.title: Array index taken from a query string sizes an unbounded slice allocation in deepObject decoding

location.component: openapi3filter.sliceMapToSlice, reached from urlValuesDecoder.DecodeObject -> makeObject -> buildResObj

findings.evidence: sliceMapToSlice (openapi3filter/req_resp_decoder.go:936-962) parses every map key as an integer with strconv.Atoi (:941), takes the maximum (:947-952) and then grows a slice one element at a time from 0 to that maximum (:953-960). The keys are the bracketed segments of a query-parameter name: urlValuesDecoder.DecodeObject's deepObject branch (:661-681) extracts them with the `\[(.*?)\]` capture at :669 and joins them into props; makeObject (:911) turns them into nested maps with deepSet (:899-909); buildResObj's array branch (:965-993) hands that map to sliceMapToSlice and then allocates a second slice of the same length with make([]any, len(arr)) at :986. Nothing between the socket and :953 compares the index against a bound. Concretely, for a query parameter declared `style: deepObject` whose schema is an object with an array property `arr`, the request `?p[arr][2147483647]=x` makes max = 2147483647 and drives the loop at :953 to append ~2.1e9 interface values (about 34 GB on a 64-bit build) before any schema keyword, including maxItems, is ever consulted; validation of the decoded value happens later, in ValidateParameter at openapi3filter/validate_request.go:245. maxItems is therefore not a control here: it runs after the allocation. The same handler additionally calls regexp.MustCompile twice per query-string key (:665 and :669), inside the loop over every parameter in the request.
findings.impact: An unauthenticated remote client crashes the server process with a single short request: Go's out-of-memory condition is a fatal runtime error that net/http's per-connection recover cannot catch, so this is process termination and not merely a dropped connection. The index costs the attacker ten bytes and costs the server gigabytes, and the request can be repeated concurrently.
findings.preconditions: The application validates requests with openapi3filter (ValidateRequest / ValidateParameter or the Validator middleware) against a document that declares at least one query parameter with `style: deepObject` whose schema is an object containing an array-typed property, or an object with additionalProperties resolving to an array. No credential, no session and no non-default library option is required.
findings.recommendation: Bound the index before it sizes anything: in sliceMapToSlice, reject an index above a configured maximum (and above len(m) plus a small slack, since a sparse array whose highest index far exceeds the number of supplied elements is not a legitimate encoding), and reject negative values, before entering the loop at :953. Applying schema.MaxItems at decode time, where it is available on the SchemaRef already being passed down, would give the operator a per-parameter bound with no new API. Separately, hoist the two regular expressions at :665 and :669 into package-level variables so they are compiled once rather than twice per query-string key.

triage.reason: The only candidate control is the schema's maxItems keyword, and it is applied in openapi3/schema.go:2760 during visitJSONArray, which runs from ValidateParameter (openapi3filter/validate_request.go:245) only after decodeStyledParameter has already returned the decoded slice. The allocation precedes every keyword check.

The index is a substring of a query-parameter name, taken from input.GetQueryParams() (openapi3filter/validate_request_input.go:31-37, backed by http.Request.URL.Query()), and reaches strconv.Atoi at :941 with no allowlist or normalisation in between.
The second principal is any remote HTTP client; the boundary crossed is client to server process, in an unauthenticated request-validation path.
The attacker gains process termination they did not previously have; this is not a defence-in-depth gap.

findings.limits: The 34 GB figure is arithmetic (2^31 interface values at 16 bytes each on a 64-bit build), not a measurement: no Go toolchain was available on the audit host, so the allocation was not executed. What is established by reading is that no bound exists between the query string and the loop bound, not the exact byte count at which a given deployment dies.
findings.unaided_label: deepObject array index sizes an unbounded allocation

findings.title: PathItem.GetOperation panics on any unrecognised HTTP method and the legacy router reaches it with the client's method
findings.evidence: GetOperation (openapi3/path_item.go:153-175) switches over the nine methods named in net/http and its default arm is `panic(fmt.Errorf("unsupported HTTP method %q", method))` at :174. routers/legacy/router.go:108-153 calls it with the raw request method: FindRoute takes `method := req.Method` (:109), asks the pathpattern tree for a match (:141) and, when no route came back, looks the path up directly and calls `pathItem.GetOperation(method)` at :150. The tree cannot absorb an unknown method: CreateNode registers every route as the literal string `METHOD + " " + path` (routers/legacy/router.go:70) and matchRemaining compares constant prefixes (routers/legacy/pathpattern/node.go:275-281), so `FOO /pets` matches no `GET `/`POST ` prefix, Match returns nil, and control reaches :146. Paths.Value(remainingPath) returns the PathItem for any statically declared path, and :150 then panics. An HTTP token such as FOO is a legal method on the wire and Go's net/http server passes it through unmodified. The same construct exists in openapi2/path_item.go:129 and :150 and in openapi3/path_item.go:199 (SetOperation); no request-time caller was found for those three.
findings.impact: An unauthenticated remote client aborts request handling with `curl -X FOO http://host/<a static path from the spec>`. Under net/http the panic is caught by the per-connection recover, so the connection is reset with no response and a full stack trace is written to the server log: repeated at rate this is log amplification and wasted CPU, not process death. Outside a net/http handler goroutine - a framework without panic recovery, or an application that calls FindRoute from a worker, a warm-up or a batch job - the same call terminates the process.
findings.preconditions: The application routes with routers/legacy (Router.FindRoute or Routers.FindRoute) and the document declares at least one path with no template variables, so Paths.Value can match the request path literally. The gorillamux router is not affected: its mux route carries a Methods(...) matcher, so FindRoute only reaches GetOperation for a method the document declares.
findings.recommendation: Make GetOperation total: return nil from the default arm instead of panicking, which is the contract every caller already assumes (routers/legacy/router.go:150 immediately tests the result for nil). Keep the panic, if it is wanted at all, in SetOperation, where the argument is programmer-supplied. As defence in depth, have routers/legacy normalise or reject a method outside the known set before line 150. Also add a regression test that calls FindRoute with a method such as `FOO` and asserts routers.ErrMethodNotAllowed rather than a panic.

triage.reason: No control stands between req.Method and :150. net/http's per-connection recover does not prevent the panic and does not sit on the path to the sink; it bounds the blast radius only, and its effect is stated in impact rather than used to close the finding.
The value is http.Request.Method, copied verbatim at routers/legacy/router.go:109 and passed to GetOperation at :150 with no normalisation or allowlist.
routers/legacy is an exported package of the published module with no build tag; routers/legacy/router.go is ordinary shipped code and is documented in .github/docs/routers_legacy.txt.
The second principal is any remote HTTP client; the boundary crossed is client to server process, before any authentication runs.
The construct is what it looks like: an explicit panic in the default arm of a method switch, at openapi3/path_item.go:174.

findings.limits: This establishes that the panic is reachable, not that it kills the process in a given deployment: under Go's net/http server the standard per-connection recover contains it. It also does not establish the neighbouring nil dereference at routers/legacy/router.go:158, where `node.VariableNames` is read after the nil check on `route` rather than on `node`; that line is reachable only if GetOperation returns non-nil while Match returned nil, and no input producing that combination was constructed.
findings.unaided_label: legacy router panics on an unrecognised HTTP method

findings.title: Nil regular-expression matcher is dereferenced when a schema pattern fails to compile and MultiError is enabled
findings.evidence: visitJSONString's pattern block (openapi3/schema.go:2654-2669) loads a cached matcher, and on a miss calls compilePattern at :2659. When compilation fails and settings.multiError is set, the error is appended to the accumulator at :2662 and execution continues to `if !cp.MatchString(value)` at :2666. cp is not usable at that point: compilePattern (openapi3/schema_pattern.go:16-32) assigns the result of regexp.Compile into the named return `cp RegexMatcher` at :21, so on failure cp holds a typed nil *regexp.Regexp - a non-nil interface whose method call dereferences a nil receiver - and the error arm returns at :31 without clearing it. With a custom RegexCompilerFunc (:19) the same line yields whatever the compiler returned, commonly an untyped nil interface, which also panics on the call. The non-MultiError path is unaffected because :2661 returns first.
findings.impact: Every request carrying a string value for the affected property panics inside request validation. Under net/http the connection is reset with no response and a stack trace is logged; outside a recovered handler goroutine the process terminates. The panic is triggered by ordinary traffic, so it is a permanent outage of that operation rather than an attacker-timed event.
findings.preconditions: Two things must be true together. First, the document reaches request validation carrying a `pattern` the Go regexp engine rejects - ECMA-only constructs such as lookahead `(?=`, lookbehind `(?<=` and backreferences are the common case - which happens when the document was never passed through openapi3.T.Validate (routers/gorillamux.NewRouter does not call it; its doc comment only assumes the caller did) or was validated with DisableSchemaPatternValidation, since that option is a document-validation option and does not set the separate request-time flag schemaValidationSettings.patternValidationDisabled. Second, validation runs with MultiError - openapi3filter.Options.MultiError, which becomes openapi3.MultiErrors() at openapi3filter/validate_request.go:237 and :341.
findings.recommendation: In visitJSONString, do not fall through to :2666 when compilePattern returned an error: skip the pattern check for that schema after recording the error, or return the accumulated MultiError. In compilePattern, set cp to nil explicitly on the error path so a caller that ignores err cannot get a typed-nil matcher, and reject a compiler that returns (nil, nil). A regression test that calls visitJSONString with MultiErrors() on a schema whose Pattern is `(?=x)` fails today and passes after the fix.

triage.reason: openapi3.T.Validate does compile patterns (openapi3/schema.go:1684-1688), but it is a control the caller may forget - routers/gorillamux.NewRouter never invokes it - and DisableSchemaPatternValidation lets a document pass validation while request-time pattern checking stays on. FP-01 excludes a control a caller may skip.

The value that reaches the sink at :2666 is the request string being validated, taken from the decoded parameter or body. The compile failure is a property of the document rather than of the attacker, which is why it is stated as a precondition and why the severity is low.
The sink is a method call on an interface value, at openapi3/schema.go:2666; there is no form of it that is safe with a nil receiver.
openapi3/schema.go is the core shipped file of the module; the block is not behind a build tag or a debug flag.
The second principal is the remote HTTP client whose request triggers the validation; the boundary crossed is client to server process.

findings.limits: Severity is held at low because the crash condition is chosen by whoever writes the document, not by the attacker, and because both preconditions must coincide. Nothing here was executed: the typed-nil behaviour of regexp.Compile's error return and the resulting nil-receiver panic are read from the assignment at openapi3/schema_pattern.go:21, not observed.
findings.unaided_label: nil regex matcher dereferenced when a schema pattern fails to compile under MultiError

findings.title: Decoding an array parameter whose schema omits items dereferences a nil SchemaRef
findings.evidence: parseArray (openapi3filter/req_resp_decoder.go:1103-1120) passes schemaRef.Value.Items straight to parsePrimitive at :1106, and parsePrimitive's first statement (:1128) is `schema.Value.Type.Slice()`. When the array schema has no `items`, Items is nil and that line dereferences a nil *openapi3.SchemaRef. urlValuesDecoder.parseArray does the same at :555 into parseValue, whose first statement reads schema.Value.AllOf. All four decoders reach it: pathParamDecoder.DecodeArray (:394), urlValuesDecoder.DecodeArray (:522), headerParamDecoder.DecodeArray (:744) and cookieParamDecoder.DecodeArray (:805), each selected by decodeValue at :323 whenever the parameter schema's type is `array`. The document is not rejected first: Schema.validate only requires `items` for arrays when 2020-12 validation is off (openapi3/schema.go:1690, `if schema.Items == nil && !validationOpts.jsonSchema2020ValidationEnabled && len(schema.PrefixItems) == 0`), and T.Validate turns that flag on for every 3.1 document (openapi3/openapi3.go:269-270 into openapi3/validation_options.go:41-42). A 3.1 document declaring `type: array` with no `items` - legal JSON Schema, where items defaults to true - therefore passes Validate and panics on the first request that supplies the parameter.
findings.impact: Any request supplying that parameter aborts request handling. Under net/http the connection is reset with no response and a stack trace is logged; outside a recovered handler goroutine the process terminates. Because the trigger is ordinary traffic rather than a crafted value, the affected operation is unusable rather than intermittently attackable.
findings.preconditions: An OpenAPI 3.1 document (or a 3.0 document that skipped T.Validate) declaring a path, query, header or cookie parameter whose schema is `type: array` with no `items` and no `prefixItems`, validated through openapi3filter. No credential is required to trigger it.
findings.recommendation: Treat a missing items schema as 'no per-item constraint' rather than as a schema: in parseArray and urlValuesDecoder.parseArray, when schemaRef.Value.Items is nil, return the raw strings unchanged instead of calling parsePrimitive. Defensively, have parsePrimitive and parseValue return a ParseError when their schema argument or its Value is nil, so no future caller can reintroduce the dereference. A regression test with a 3.1 document and a bare `type: array` parameter fails today.

triage.reason: The candidate control is the items-required check at openapi3/schema.go:1690, and it is disabled by construction for 3.1 documents because T.Validate sets jsonSchema2020ValidationEnabled at openapi3/validation_options.go:42.
The parameter value arrives from the query string, a path segment, a header or a cookie and reaches parseArray unmodified; the nil that is dereferenced is reached by supplying that parameter at all.
openapi3filter/req_resp_decoder.go is shipped, unconditioned code, and the four DecodeArray call sites are the ordinary decoding path used by ValidateParameter.
The second principal is any remote HTTP client; the boundary crossed is client to server process, before authentication.

findings.limits: Not executed. The claim that a 3.1 document with a bare `type: array` survives T.Validate rests on reading the three lines that gate it (openapi3/schema.go:1690, openapi3/openapi3.go:269-270, openapi3/validation_options.go:41-42), not on running Validate. Severity is held at low because the defect needs a particular, if entirely legal, schema shape.
findings.unaided_label: array parameter whose schema omits items dereferences a nil SchemaRef

findings.title: GitHub Actions workflows declare no permissions block while exposing GITHUB_TOKEN to every step
findings.evidence: Neither .github/workflows/go.yml nor .github/workflows/shellcheck.yml contains a `permissions:` key at workflow or job level, so both inherit whatever default the repository or organization sets for GITHUB_TOKEN. go.yml additionally lifts the token into the job environment at :10 (`GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}`), which makes it visible to every step of build-and-test rather than only to the steps that need it - and those steps include third-party code fetched at run time (`go run golang.org/x/tools/.../modernize@latest` at :59, `go run golang.org/x/tools/.../nilness@latest` at :99, `go install github.com/incu6us/goimports-reviser/v3@latest` at :202) and `go generate ./...` at :45. Both workflows trigger on `push` as well as `pull_request` (go.yml:3-4, shellcheck.yml:3-5), so the token in a push run is the repository's own, not a fork's read-only one.
findings.impact: If the repository default is read-write - the platform default unless changed - then any code that executes inside build-and-test holds a token that can write repository contents, and the workflow deliberately executes third-party code from mutable @latest references. The consequence of a compromised upstream tool is not a failed build but a writable repository.
findings.preconditions: A push to the repository (or a merge) runs the workflow with the repository's GITHUB_TOKEN. The severity depends entirely on the default workflow permission configured outside the tree.
findings.recommendation: Add `permissions: contents: read` at the top of both workflows and grant anything beyond that per job, at the job that needs it. Remove `GITHUB_TOKEN` from the job-level `env:` in go.yml:10 and pass it only to the step that requires it, so a compromised @latest tool does not inherit it.
findings.inference: That the effective default GITHUB_TOKEN permission for this repository is read-write. That setting lives in the GitHub repository or organization configuration, not in the tree, and INF-15 requires the artifact rather than an assumption in either direction.
findings.what_would_settle_it: The value of Settings > Actions > General > Workflow permissions for the repository (or the organization ruleset that pins it), or a run log line showing the token scopes granted to build-and-test.

triage.reason: The second principal is the maintainer of any @latest module the workflow runs (golang.org/x/tools and github.com/incu6us/goimports-reviser); the boundary crossed is third-party code to repository write credential.

The control that would settle this - the organization or repository default workflow permission - lives outside the repository and no artifact for it was provided. FP-08 forbids answering HOLDS without that evidence, which is why the status is probable rather than confirmed.

findings.limits: This does not establish that the token is currently read-write, only that the workflows do not constrain it and that they hand it to code they do not control. If the default is already read-only, the finding drops to hardening without changing the recommendation.
findings.unaided_label: CI workflows declare no permissions block

findings.title: CI executes third-party actions by mutable tag and Go tools by @latest
findings.evidence: Not one `uses:` in either workflow is pinned by commit SHA: go.yml references actions/setup-go@v6 (:28, :199), actions/cache@v3 (:33), actions/checkout@v6 (:43, :198); shellcheck.yml references actions/checkout@v2 (:12) and ludeeus/action-shellcheck@1.1.0 (:15). That is 0 of 7 `uses:` references pinned, across 5 distinct actions. Three steps go further and resolve third-party Go modules at run time from a floating pointer: `go run golang.org/x/tools/go/analysis/passes/modernize/cmd/modernize@latest -test -diff -fix` at go.yml:59, which is invoked with `-fix` and therefore rewrites the checked-out tree; `go run golang.org/x/tools/go/analysis/passes/nilness/cmd/nilness@latest` at :99; and `go install github.com/incu6us/goimports-reviser/v3@latest` at :202, whose binary is then run over every Go file at :204. `@latest` and a git tag are both mutable pointers: the code that runs tomorrow need not be the code that ran today, and go.mod/go.sum do not cover any of it because none of these tools is a module dependency.
findings.impact: Whoever controls one of those upstream repositories, or a tag on them, executes arbitrary code inside the CI job on every push and pull request. The job holds GITHUB_TOKEN in its environment (go.yml:10, see F-005) and its working tree is the repository being built, so a compromised tool can both read the token and modify the source it is asked to format.
findings.preconditions: None inside this repository: the exposure exists on every workflow run. Exploitation requires compromise of, or a malicious release from, one of the referenced third parties.
findings.recommendation: Pin every `uses:` to a full 40-character commit SHA with the version in a trailing comment, and let Dependabot or Renovate bump them. Replace the three `@latest` invocations with a pinned version - either an explicit `@vX.Y.Z` or, better, a tools.go plus go.mod entry so go.sum covers the checksum. Give the `-fix` step in particular a pinned version, since it is authorised to rewrite the tree.

triage.reason: There is no pinning policy, no allowlist and no verification step anywhere in .github/; the two workflow files are the whole CI configuration in the tree.

The second principal is a third party outside this repository's access-control perimeter: ludeeus, golang.org/x/tools and github.com/incu6us. Only actions/* is a first-party-adjacent publisher, and it is still a different owner.

This is not a missing defence in depth: the unpinned code runs with a repository token in its environment and, in the modernize step, with permission to rewrite the tree. The impact reaches the repository, not just the build.

findings.limits: The count of unpinned references is exact; the risk is a supply-chain exposure and not a demonstrated compromise - no evidence was sought or found that any of these upstreams is malicious today, and no network lookup was permitted to check their current state.
findings.unaided_label: CI runs third-party actions and @latest Go tools that are not pinned

findings.title: ZipFileBodyDecoder appends the whole read buffer regardless of bytes read, and decompresses without a bound
findings.evidence: The read loop at openapi3filter/req_resp_decoder.go:1636-1647 does `n, err := rc.Read(buffer)` and then, on `if 0 < n`, `content = append(content, buffer...)` at :1639 - the whole 256-byte buffer rather than buffer[:n]. Every short read therefore contributes 256 bytes to the decoded value: trailing zero bytes on the first pass and, on later passes, the residue of whatever was read before, including bytes from the previous entry of the same archive. The decoded string handed to schema validation is consequently not the archive's content. In the same function the capacity at :1623 is `make([]byte, 0, bufferSize*len(zr.File))`, sized from the entry count declared in the uploaded archive, and the loop from :1626 concatenates every entry with no ceiling on the total; the doc comment at :1608-1609 acknowledges this second half ('Use with caution as this implementation may be susceptible to a zip bomb attack').
findings.impact: Any consumer that registers this decoder validates a body that differs from what was uploaded: bytes the client never sent are appended, and content from one archive entry bleeds into the decoded value of another within the same request. A schema check performed on that value is a check on the wrong bytes, so it can both reject valid input and accept input the archive did not contain.
findings.preconditions: The application calls openapi3filter.RegisterBodyDecoder with ZipFileBodyDecoder; it is exported but not registered by the package's own init (openapi3filter/req_resp_decoder.go:1334-1348). Any entry whose length is not an exact multiple of 256, or any read that returns short, triggers it - which is the normal case.
findings.recommendation: Append buffer[:n] at :1639. Then bound the decompression: keep a running total across entries, compare it against a caller-supplied maximum before each append, and abort with a ParseError when it is exceeded; also reject an archive whose declared entry count would make the :1623 capacity unreasonable, since that value comes from the uploaded file. If the decoder is meant to stay a sample rather than a supported path, say so in the doc comment and stop exporting it.

triage.reason: Nothing between :1636 and :1647 bounds n, the per-entry total or the archive total; the only guard in the function is the loop's io.EOF break.
Both the entry count read at :1623 and the per-entry lengths that make reads short come from the uploaded archive, which is the request body.
ZipFileBodyDecoder is an exported symbol of the shipped package and appears in .github/docs/openapi3filter.txt; it is opt-in, not absent.
The doc comment at :1608 warns about zip bombs only. It says nothing about the buffer defect at :1639, so the corrupted output is not an intended, bounded exposure.
The second principal is the remote client uploading the archive; the boundary crossed is client to the validation decision made about that client's own request.
The impact reaches the consumer's validation decision, which is the control the library exists to provide; it is not a defence-in-depth gap.

findings.limits: Severity is held at low because the decoder is opt-in and, for the compression half, the doc comment already warns. The concrete claim established here is the buffer defect at :1639; what a corrupted decoded value does downstream depends on the consumer's schema and handler and is not established.
findings.unaided_label: ZipFileBodyDecoder appends the whole read buffer and decompresses without a bound

findings.title: Schema validation errors embed the failing value and the full schema by default

location.component: openapi3.SchemaError.Error and the SchemaErrorDetailsDisabled package variable

findings.evidence: SchemaError.Error (openapi3/schema.go:3086-3132) ends with `if !SchemaErrorDetailsDisabled` at :3120 and then JSON-encodes both the schema (:3124) and the offending value (:3128) into the message. SchemaErrorDetailsDisabled is declared false at openapi3/schema.go:34, so details are on unless the consumer flips a package-level global. The struct's own comment on the Reason field (:3038) states the opposite intent - 'The message should never include the original value to prevent leakage of potentially sensitive inputs in error messages' - which the Value block at :3127-3129 contradicts. The error text is not confined to logs: openapi3filter/validation_error_encoder.go:74-78 puts e.Error() into ValidationError.Title, and openapi3filter/errors.go composes RequestError messages from the wrapped cause.
findings.impact: A consumer that returns the validation error to the caller - which ConvertErrors and ValidationErrorEncoder exist to make easy - echoes the rejected value back, and with it the internal schema, including property names, formats, patterns and bounds that were not otherwise published. The rejected value is frequently the sensitive one: a password that failed a pattern, a token that failed a format.
findings.preconditions: Default library configuration; no option needs to be set. The disclosure reaches an outside party only if the consumer surfaces the error text, which openapi3filter.Validator's own default errFunc (openapi3filter/middleware.go:64-66) deliberately does not do - it writes only a generic status text.
findings.recommendation: Invert the default: emit the schema and the value only when a consumer opts in, and make the opt-in a per-validation option rather than a package-level global that one dependency can flip for the whole process. Until then, document on ValidationErrorEncoder and ConvertErrors that their output is not safe to return verbatim, and honour the stated intent of the Reason comment by keeping the value out of the message.

triage.reason: The available controls - setting SchemaErrorDetailsDisabled or passing SetSchemaErrorMessageCustomizer - are ones the caller may simply not know about, and FP-01 excludes a control a caller may forget.
The disclosed value is whatever the client sent for the failing property, which may be a credential; it is not public or synthetic data by construction.

Whether anything reaches an attacker is decided by the consumer's error handler, and this library's own middleware default (openapi3filter/middleware.go:64-66) does not return the text. The defect is the insecure default, so it is recorded as hardening at informational severity rather than as an exploit path.

findings.limits: No exploit path is asserted inside this repository. Establishing one requires a consumer application whose error handler returns the message, and no such consumer is in scope.
findings.unaided_label: schema error text embeds the failing value and the full schema by default

findings.title: External $ref resolution reads any local path and any HTTP URL with no allowlist hook short of replacing the reader
findings.evidence: DefaultReadFromURI (openapi3/loader_uri_reader.go:46) chains ReadFromHTTP(http.DefaultClient) and ReadFromFile. ReadFromHTTP (:51-70) issues a GET to whatever URL the document names, with the default client - which follows up to ten redirects - and no scheme, host, port or address check; ReadFromFile (:79-84) calls os.ReadFile on path.Clean of the document's path with no base-directory containment. The gate is the single boolean IsExternalRefsAllowed, checked at openapi3/loader.go:118-120 and :348-350, with the test itself at :107-112, and it is all-or-nothing: there is no hook to allow one host or one directory. It is also skipped entirely when a custom ReadFromURIFunc is installed (openapi3/loader.go:118 and :348), which the field's own comment documents as a security-relevant delegation (openapi3/loader.go:39-48). Relative refs are joined with defaultJoin (:298-305) using path.Join, which cleans `..` upward, so a relative $ref resolves above the document's own directory.
findings.impact: A consumer that loads documents it did not write - an API gateway ingesting a customer-supplied spec, a linting service, a CI job validating an untrusted file - and enables external refs gives the document author a read primitive over the process's filesystem (`$ref: "/etc/passwd"`) and an outbound request from the server's network position (`$ref: "http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/"`), with the fetched bytes surfaced through the parsed document or through the parse error.
findings.preconditions: Loader.IsExternalRefsAllowed set to true, or a custom ReadFromURIFunc that delegates to DefaultReadFromURI, together with a document from an untrusted source. cmd/validate leaves the flag off by default (cmd/validate/main.go:26-28, :63), so the shipped CLI is not affected unless --ext is passed.
findings.recommendation: Give the loader a bounded policy rather than a boolean: an optional allowlist of schemes, hosts and a base directory that ReadFromHTTP and ReadFromFile consult, so a consumer can enable external refs without granting the whole filesystem and network. Make ReadFromFile verify that the resolved path is still inside the document's root after cleaning, and give ReadFromHTTP a client with redirects disabled or re-validated per hop and an explicit timeout. Keep the existing warning on ReadFromURIFunc, and repeat it on IsExternalRefsAllowed itself, which today carries no such note.

triage.reason: IsExternalRefsAllowed is a switch, not a bound: once true, the test at openapi3/loader.go:107-112 permits every reference, and no allowlist exists anywhere in openapi3/loader_uri_reader.go.
The URL is the $ref string from the document, which in the threat model that makes this matter is written by the party supplying the document.

The exposure is intended: the field is documented as 'enables visiting other files' and the SECURITY note at openapi3/loader.go:39-48 names local file read and SSRF explicitly. Per FP-05 the finding moves rather than disappearing - it moves to the absence of any bound behind the intended exposure, which is what the recommendation addresses.
The second principal is the author of a document the operator did not write; the boundary crossed is document to host filesystem and to the host's network position.

findings.limits: No exploit is asserted against this repository: the risk exists only in a consumer that both enables external refs and loads untrusted documents. The behaviour of http.DefaultClient's redirect handling is standard-library behaviour, read from the absence of any CheckRedirect assignment at openapi3/loader_uri_reader.go:51-70 rather than observed.
findings.unaided_label: external $ref resolution reads local files and remote URLs with no allowlist

findings.title: AWS access key identifier present in a vendored OpenAPI test fixture

location.component: vendored third-party specification used as a test fixture

findings.evidence: A working-tree scan for the distinctive credential formats named in SUP-16 (GitHub personal, OAuth, user, server and refresh tokens; AWS access key identifiers; Anthropic API keys; Slack tokens; Google API keys; and PEM private-key headers), run over the whole target excluding .git, returned exactly one hit: line 29766 of openapi3/testdata/oai_v3_stoplight.json carries an example S3 pre-signed URL containing `X-Amz-Credential=[REDACTED:secret]` and `X-Amz-Signature=[REDACTED:secret]` alongside `X-Amz-Date=20170728...` and `X-Amz-Expires=3600`. The surrounding document is a vendored third-party API specification kept as a parser fixture; the string is an example value inside it, not configuration this project reads. No hit was found anywhere in non-test Go source for password, secret, token or api-key literals.
findings.impact: None demonstrated. An AWS access key identifier is not by itself a credential - the secret access key is what authenticates - and the accompanying signature is scoped to one object and one hour, both of which elapsed in 2017. The fact is recorded so a future scanner hit on this line is triaged once rather than repeatedly.
findings.recommendation: No rotation is called for and none should be attempted; the identifier belongs to a third party. If the repository adopts a secret-scanning gate, add this path to its allowlist with the reason, so the finding is closed deliberately instead of being muted wholesale.

triage.reason: The value is an example inside a vendored third-party specification at openapi3/testdata/oai_v3_stoplight.json:29766, carried as parser input; nothing in this project reads it as configuration.
The string is an AWS access key identifier rather than a secret access key, and the pre-signed signature beside it declares X-Amz-Expires=3600 against a 2017 date, so it authorises nothing now.

findings.limits: The scan covered the working tree only. Secrets in git history were not looked for: reading history was excluded by the engagement instruction, so SUP-17 was not exercised and silence about it is silence. The value was never tested against any service.
findings.unaided_label: AWS access key id inside a vendored test fixture

findings.title: OpenAPI 3.1 validation recompiles the whole JSON Schema on every request
findings.evidence: VisitJSON dispatches to useJSONSchema2020 whenever the caller passed EnableJSONSchema2020 (openapi3/schema.go:1942-1948), and useJSONSchema2020 calls newJSONSchemaValidator(schema) at openapi3/schema_jsonschema_validator.go:205 on every invocation. That constructor marshals the entire schema to JSON (:21), unmarshals it back into a map (:27), walks the whole tree rewriting keywords (:32, recursive at :116/:126/:137), builds a brand-new jsonschema.Compiler (:35) and compiles the resource (:45). Nothing is memoised: the only cache in the package is compiledPatterns (openapi3/schema.go:46), which holds individual `pattern` regexps and is not consulted here, and the constructed validator is discarded when useJSONSchema2020 returns. openapi3filter takes this path for every 3.1 document and on every request: EnableJSONSchema2020 is appended at openapi3filter/validate_request.go:242-244 for each parameter and at :354-356 for the body, and at openapi3filter/validate_response.go:76-78 for responses.
findings.impact: For an OpenAPI 3.1 document, each request pays a CPU cost proportional to the size of the resolved schema for the parameter or body it targets - a full marshal, unmarshal, recursive rewrite and schema compilation, including recompilation of every `pattern` in that subtree. An unauthenticated client turns a small request into that fixed work, repeatedly and concurrently, which is an amplification factor rather than a constant overhead. It also means the pattern cache the library maintains for the 3.0 path buys nothing on the 3.1 path.
findings.preconditions: The document declares `openapi: 3.1.x` (openapi3/openapi3.go:49-57 decides this), and requests are validated through openapi3filter. No option needs to be enabled: openapi3filter turns on the 2020-12 path automatically for 3.1 documents.
findings.recommendation: Compile once per schema and reuse. Cache the compiled *jsonschema.Schema keyed by the *openapi3.Schema pointer, in a sync.Map alongside compiledPatterns, or build the validator when the document is loaded and hang it off the schema. Either removes the per-request marshal-and-compile entirely; the existing compiledPatterns cache is the precedent for the shape of the fix.

triage.reason: No cache stands between VisitJSON and the compiler: grep for compiledPatterns across the package finds it referenced only at openapi3/schema.go:46, :2655 and openapi3/schema_pattern.go:34, none of which is on the 2020-12 path.
The attacker controls how often the work happens: every request that reaches ValidateParameter or ValidateRequestBody triggers a fresh compilation.
The second principal is any remote HTTP client; the boundary crossed is client to server CPU, before authentication in the middleware ordering.
The attacker gains an amplification factor proportional to schema size that they did not previously hold; this is not a missing defence in depth.

findings.limits: The absence of caching is established by reading; the size of the amplification is not measured, because no Go toolchain was available to benchmark it. How much it matters depends on the size of the schema subtree reached by a given operation, which is a property of the consumer's document.
findings.unaided_label: OpenAPI 3.1 validation recompiles the JSON Schema on every call

findings.title: OpenAPI 3.1 validation fails open to a validator that ignores every 2020-12 keyword
findings.evidence: useJSONSchema2020 (openapi3/schema_jsonschema_validator.go:204-212) discards the constructor's error - `if err != nil { return schema.visitJSON(settings, value) }` at :206-209, with the comment 'Fall back to built-in validator if compilation fails'. Nothing is logged and nothing is returned to the caller, so a document whose 2020-12 schema will not compile is validated by the built-in engine and reports success. The built-in engine implements none of the 2020-12 keywords: visitJSON (openapi3/schema.go:1951-2048) handles not, oneOf, anyOf, allOf, enum and const before dispatching by type; visitJSONObject (:2831-2993) handles properties, minProperties, maxProperties, additionalProperties and required; visitJSONArray (:2732-2823) handles minItems, maxItems, uniqueItems and items. The fields If, Then, Else, DependentRequired, DependentSchemas, PatternProperties, PropertyNames, PrefixItems, Contains, MinContains, MaxContains, UnevaluatedItems and UnevaluatedProperties are declared on the Schema struct (openapi3/schema.go:138-152) and appear in marshalling (:614-651), in JSONLookup (:880-945), in IsEmpty (:1296-1364) and in spec validation (:1444-1489) - but in no visitJSON* function. A likely trigger for the fallback is ordinary: newJSONSchemaValidator adds a single resource whose body is the marshalled schema (:39-42), and SchemaRef.MarshalYAML emits `{"$ref": "..."}` for any reference that was kept (openapi3/refs.go:1049-1054), so a nested `$ref: "#/components/schemas/Foo"` becomes a pointer into a resource that contains no components object.
findings.impact: Constraints the document author wrote are silently not enforced. An input that an `if/then/else` branch, a `dependentRequired` rule, a `patternProperties` restriction or a `contains` bound was meant to reject is accepted by the validator, and the application behind it receives data it believes was checked. The failure is silent by construction: no error, no log line, no difference visible to the caller.
findings.preconditions: An OpenAPI 3.1 document validated through openapi3filter (which enables the 2020-12 path automatically) whose schema for a parameter, body or response fails to compile in santhosh-tekuri/jsonschema v6 - and which relies on at least one 2020-12-only keyword for a constraint that matters.
findings.recommendation: Do not fail open. Return the compilation error to the caller, or at minimum surface it once at load time so the operator learns that a schema cannot be enforced, rather than silently substituting a weaker engine at request time. If a fallback must remain, make it explicit and opt-in, and have it report which keywords were dropped. Independently, either implement the 2020-12 keywords in the built-in validator or make it refuse a schema that carries one, so that the two engines can never disagree about whether a constraint applies.
findings.inference: That newJSONSchemaValidator's Compile step actually fails for a schema containing a nested `$ref` - and more generally, how often it fails in practice. github.com/santhosh-tekuri/jsonschema/v6 is a go.mod dependency and its source is not present in the tree (no vendor directory) and could not be fetched or executed, so its behaviour when resolving `#/components/...` against a single added resource was reasoned about rather than observed. Everything else in this finding - that the error is discarded, and that the fallback engine implements none of the 2020-12 keywords - was read directly.
findings.what_would_settle_it: A test calling openapi3.Schema.VisitJSON with EnableJSONSchema2020() on a 3.1 schema whose property is `{"$ref": "#/components/schemas/Foo"}`, asserting whether newJSONSchemaValidator returns an error; or reading the $ref resolution in github.com/santhosh-tekuri/jsonschema/v6 compiler.go at the version pinned in go.sum.

triage.reason: The fallback at openapi3/schema_jsonschema_validator.go:208 is on the only path; there is no second enforcement layer, and the built-in engine reached by that line is the weaker of the two.
The sink is the validation verdict returned to openapi3filter, which decides whether the request is accepted; a nil return there is an acceptance, not a diagnostic.
openapi3/schema_jsonschema_validator.go ships unconditionally and openapi3filter selects it for every 3.1 document at openapi3filter/validate_request.go:242-244.

The behaviour that decides how often the fallback fires belongs to a dependency outside this repository, github.com/santhosh-tekuri/jsonschema/v6, whose source was not available to read and which could not be executed. FP-08 forbids answering HOLDS without that artifact, and it is why the status is probable.

findings.limits: This does not establish the rate at which the fallback fires, only that when it fires the enforcement gap is total for 2020-12-only keywords. It also does not establish any consequence beyond 'the constraint is not applied': what an unvalidated value does downstream is the consumer application's business.
findings.unaided_label: OpenAPI 3.1 validation falls back silently when compilation fails

findings.title: Request body is buffered twice in memory when a security requirement is validated
findings.evidence: validateSecurityRequirement reads the whole request body into `data` with io.ReadAll at openapi3filter/validate_request.go:448, then restores req.Body from a closure that captures that same slice (:485-488). ValidateRequest then calls ValidateRequestBody, which reads the body again into a second slice at :271 and installs a second capturing closure at :288-290. Both slices are reachable while the second read is in flight, so peak resident size for the body is twice its length. Neither call site bounds the read: there is no MaxBytesReader, no ContentLength check and no configurable maximum anywhere in openapi3filter/options.go.
findings.impact: A constant-factor increase in the memory a request costs the server, on top of an unbounded read that the consumer is expected to cap. It gives an attacker nothing they did not already have from sending a large body.
findings.preconditions: The operation or the document declares a security requirement, so validateSecurityRequirement runs before ValidateRequestBody, and the request carries a body.
findings.recommendation: Read the body once in ValidateRequest and share the buffer with both validateSecurityRequirement and ValidateRequestBody rather than reading it twice. Separately, document that callers must wrap req.Body in http.MaxBytesReader before calling ValidateRequest, since the package offers no size limit of its own.

triage.reason: No cap exists in the package: openapi3filter/options.go declares no size option, and neither :271 nor :448 consults ContentLength.
The second principal is any remote HTTP client, and the boundary crossed is client to server memory.

The impact is a factor of two over a cost the attacker already imposes by sending the body, and a consumer that applies http.MaxBytesReader bounds both reads. It is recorded as hardening at informational severity rather than as an exploit path.

findings.limits: The doubling is read from the two io.ReadAll calls and the two capturing closures, not measured. Whether the absence of a package-level body limit matters at all depends on the consumer, who is expected to bound the body at the server.
findings.unaided_label: request body is buffered twice when a security requirement is validated

ruled_out.where: The module has no data-access layer at all. A grep for database/sql, sqlx, gorm, mongo, .Exec( and Query( over every non-test Go file in the tree returned no file. The bound: this settles the tree as it stands, and says nothing about a consumer that feeds a decoded value into its own query.

No non-test Go file imports os/exec or references exec.Command or syscall.Exec. The two shell scripts in the tree (maps.sh, docs.sh) are developer tooling invoked from the Makefile and CI; they interpolate no external input.

text/template appears in exactly one file, openapi3/refsgenerator.go, which is a go:generate code generator rendering openapi3/refs.tmpl at development time. No template is rendered from request data anywhere in openapi3filter or routers.

The body decoders registered by default (openapi3filter/req_resp_decoder.go:1334-1348) decode JSON and YAML into `any` or into declared structs; no decoder resolves a type name from the payload, and no gob, pickle-equivalent or reflection-driven constructor is used. The YAML path goes through github.com/oasdiff/yaml3 into `any` at :1371-1377. The bound: the santhosh-tekuri and oasdiff dependencies themselves were not read.
The module renders no HTML and ships no browser asset: no html/template import, no template.HTML value, no static directory. It emits error strings and JSON only.
